title: Understand basic soil fertility and plant nutrition

lessons.title: Soil properties and composition
lessons.html:
What soil is made of

Soil is a living mixture. A good soil contains roughly:

  • Minerals: sand, silt and clay particles from broken-down rock.
  • Organic matter: rotting plant and animal material (humus). It holds water and nutrients and feeds soil life.
  • Water: held in the pores between particles.
  • Air: also in the pores; roots need oxygen.
  • Living things: earthworms, insects, fungi and bacteria that break down organic matter and release nutrients.

Soil texture

SoilFeelProperties
SandyGritty, falls apartDrains fast, warms quickly, holds little water and few nutrients
ClaySticky when wet, hard when dryHolds water and nutrients well, can waterlog and compact
LoamMixture, crumblyGood balance of drainage and holding capacity

Many soils in South Africa are sandy and low in organic matter, and many in high-rainfall areas are acid. That is why soil testing, liming and good organic matter management are so important here.

Soil structure and pH

  • Structure is how particles clump together. Good crumb structure lets air, water and roots move. Driving on wet soil and over-tillage destroy structure and cause compaction.
  • pH measures how acid or alkaline the soil is. Most crops grow best in slightly acid to neutral soil. Very acid soil locks up nutrients and can release aluminium that damages roots. Lime is used to raise pH.

The main plant nutrients

  • Macronutrients (needed in large amounts): nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), potassium (K), plus calcium (Ca), magnesium (Mg) and sulphur (S).
  • Micronutrients (needed in small amounts): zinc, iron, manganese, boron, copper, molybdenum.

lessons.title: Taking a soil sample
lessons.html:
Why sample?

A laboratory soil analysis tells the farmer the pH and nutrient levels, so fertiliser and lime can be applied correctly. A bad sample gives a wrong answer, and the farm may waste money on fertiliser it does not need or lose yield from too little. The analysis is only as good as the sample.

Equipment

  • Soil auger or spade.
  • Clean plastic bucket (not a fertiliser bag or metal bucket that can contaminate the sample).
  • Sample bags and a waterproof marker.
  • Map of the land and a record sheet.

Steps

  1. Divide the farm into uniform areas: each sample should represent one land with the same soil, crop and history. Sample different soils separately.
  2. Avoid unusual spots: old kraals, fertiliser spill areas, field edges, roads, ant heaps, wet patches.
  3. Walk a zigzag pattern across the area and take many sub-samples (often 15 to 20 or as the lab or advisor says).
  4. Sample at the right depth, usually the topsoil (often 0 to 20 or 0 to 30 cm) and sometimes the subsoil separately, as instructed.
  5. Mix the sub-samples well in the clean bucket and remove stones and roots.
  6. Fill the bag with the amount the lab asks for.
  7. Label clearly: farm, land number, depth, date, crop.
  8. Record on the sheet and send to the laboratory promptly.

Timing

Sample at the same time of year each time, before planting and before fertiliser is applied, so results can be compared over the years. In orchards and vineyards, leaf samples are also taken at a set growth stage.

Safety

Wear boots, a hat and gloves. Watch for snakes, holes and buried pipes or cables near buildings. Wash hands after handling soil, especially near kraals.

lessons.title: Nutrient deficiencies and preparing applications
lessons.html:
Reading the plant

Plants show symptoms when they lack nutrients. Where on the plant the symptom appears gives a clue. Nutrients that move easily in the plant (N, P, K, Mg) show first on older, lower leaves, because the plant moves them to new growth. Nutrients that do not move easily (Ca, iron, zinc, boron) show on young leaves and growing points.

NutrientTypical symptoms
NitrogenPale yellow-green plants; older leaves yellow first; slow growth
PhosphorusStunted, dark green or purplish leaves, especially in young maize
PotassiumYellow or brown scorched leaf edges on older leaves
MagnesiumYellowing between the veins on older leaves, veins stay green
CalciumDamaged growing tips; blossom-end rot in tomatoes
IronYellow young leaves with green veins
ZincSmall leaves, short internodes; white bands on maize leaves

Symptoms can be confused with disease, drought, waterlogging or herbicide damage. Report what you see; the farmer or advisor confirms with soil and leaf analysis.

Preparing and measuring nutrient applications

  • Use the fertiliser and amount on the written recommendation, for example a set number of kg per hectare or grams per plant.
  • Read the bag: the numbers show nutrient content, for example a 2:3:2 (22) mixture or limestone ammonium nitrate (LAN).
  • Weigh accurately with a calibrated scale, or use a measuring cup calibrated for that product. Do not guess with a hand.
  • Work out amounts carefully. Example: 200 kg per hectare on a 0.5 ha land needs 100 kg.
  • For liquid feeds and fertigation, measure water and product accurately and mix as instructed.
  • Apply evenly where the roots can reach it; keep fertiliser off leaves and stems to avoid burning.
  • Calibrate spreaders before use.

Safety and storage

Wear gloves and a dust mask, wash hands after handling, store fertiliser dry and away from fuel and chemicals (some fertilisers are oxidisers). Never let fertiliser wash into rivers or dams.

Key points

  • Soil contains minerals, organic matter, water, air and living things.
  • Take many sub-samples in a zigzag from one uniform area, mix, label and send.
  • Mobile nutrients show deficiency on old leaves; immobile ones on young leaves.
  • Measure fertiliser accurately from the written recommendation.
  • Store fertiliser dry and away from fuel and water sources.
